doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Emily and the Singers Unlimited
summary: Mandel explains Emily began as a motif for the Julie Andrews character, and remembers admiring Gene Puerling, with whom he worked on the Manhattan Transfer album.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Right, it started with a motif that I thought fitted the character that Julie Andrews played. You know [sings Emily, Emily] I wanted to get kind of a sort of a purity in a nice ethereal way, type of feeling, it seemed to capsulize what she was to me at that time. And the song just kind of spun itself out one night.
Gene Lees tells a nice story about, The Singers Unlimited, recording of that tune.
Do you want to tell it?

He wrote in a liner note to one of The Singers Unlimited albums that one day he wanted to know a couple of chords in “Emily,” so he picked up the phone and called you and you told him what it was and he wrote it down and you said, “You got that? Now throw those away and go to, The Singers Unlimited recording and use those changes.”

Well, then I’m sure I did ‘cause I adore the way Gene Puerling writes. I was fortunate enough to work with him again on the – well not again but I mean work with him for the first time really on the Manhattan Transfer album we both wrote choral arrangements for that. In fact we split tunes, I’d write part of it, he’d write part, that sort of thing.
